NextItNet stacks residual dilated causal convolutions to capture long-range dependencies without pooling. Its architecture suggests component-specific checks: calculate the theoretical receptive-field span as R = 1 + Σ(kℓ−1)dℓ across every convolution; compare it with history lengths, then measure actual influence using lag-wise embedding gradients or item replacements. Proposed implementation checks: changing positions after t must leave log2feats(sequence)[:, t] unchanged; left-padded readout must select the largest nonzero index, never count−1. Compare identical histories under additional leading padding in evaluation mode to detect boundary contamination, including biases propagating through padding. These are diagnostic recommendations derived from the architecture, not reported benchmark findings. [NextItNet paper](https://fajieyuan.github.io/papers/nextitnet6.pdf).

Recent research supports separating recency from ordering: a [2024 study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722) measures excessive recency bias, while [CETRec (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.03047) distinguishes absolute recency and relative order in LLM recommenders. For one frozen NextItNet checkpoint/category, compare original histories with old-prefix deletion, recent-suffix deletion, and recent-order shuffling that preserves item membership; report paired target-rank changes and HR@10 changes using unchanged validation candidates. Temporarily bypass individual residual branches to localize dependence on dilation blocks. Old-prefix removal improving ranking suggests stale-history interference; negligible recent-order effects suggest weak order use, although order may be uninformative. Distinguish structural reach from learned influence: perturbations outside the receptive field cannot affect predictions; weak sensitivity inside it suggests ineffective use. Block bypass is an intervention on a trained network, not evidence of retrained performance. Padding and causality checks should pass before interpreting these effects.
